lessonTitle: Glycolysis and the Fate of Pyruvate

blocks.text: A venous blood sample left standing for hours before it reaches the laboratory shows a falling glucose and a rising lactate, even though the tube contains no organ at all. The red cells in the tube are still burning glucose. This is why glucose samples are collected into tubes containing fluoride, which inhibits the glycolytic enzyme enolase, and it shows how completely red cells depend on glycolysis.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** Glycolysis splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules in the **cytosol**, trapping some of the released energy as ATP and NADH. It needs no oxygen. It has two phases: an **investment phase** in which 2 ATP are spent to phosphorylate and split the sugar, and a **payoff phase** in which the two triose phosphates are converted to pyruvate, making 4 ATP and 2 NADH. The **net yield is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose**.

blocks.title: Glycolysis and substrate-level phosphorylation
blocks.text: Glycolysis is the cytosolic pathway converting glucose (C6) to two pyruvate (C3). ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation, in which a phosphate group is transferred directly from a high-energy intermediate (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate or phosphoenolpyruvate) to ADP, rather than by the proton gradient of oxidative phosphorylation.

blocks.markdown: **The ten steps in outline.** (1) Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase; glucokinase in liver; uses ATP). (2) Isomerisation to fructose-6-phosphate. (3) Fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (**phosphofructokinase-1, PFK-1**; uses ATP). (4) Aldolase splits it into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, which are interconverted by triose phosphate isomerase. (5) Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase makes 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and NADH. (6) Phosphoglycerate kinase makes ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate. (7) to (9) Mutase and **enolase** (inhibited by fluoride) give phosphoenolpyruvate. (10) **Pyruvate kinase** gives pyruvate and ATP. Steps 5 to 10 happen twice per glucose.

rows: Hexokinase: product glucose-6-phosphate. Glucokinase is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate and has a high Km, so it responds to blood glucose after meals
ATP, citrate (signals plenty of energy and fuel)
blocks.caption: The three irreversible, regulated enzymes of glycolysis. The other seven reactions operate near equilibrium and run in either direction.

blocks.title: ATP and NADH balance of glycolysis
blocks.prompt: Show that glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

steps.text: Investment: hexokinase uses 1 ATP and PFK-1 uses 1 ATP, so 2 ATP are consumed.
Aldolase gives two triose phosphates, so every subsequent step runs twice per glucose.
Payoff: phosphoglycerate kinase makes 2 ATP and pyruvate kinase makes 2 ATP, giving 4 ATP. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase makes 2 NADH.

blocks.answer: Net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. The NADH must be reoxidised for glycolysis to continue.

blocks.markdown: **Fates of pyruvate.** Glycolysis needs a constant supply of NAD+ for the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step. When oxygen and mitochondria are available, NADH is reoxidised by the respiratory chain (shuttle systems carry its electrons into mitochondria) and pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, where the **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH)** converts it irreversibly to acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. PDH needs five cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), lipoamide, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD+. When oxygen is lacking or there are no mitochondria, **lactate dehydrogenase** reduces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue. Lactate itself is a dead end that must be exported.

rows: CO2 and water after the citric acid cycle
blocks.caption: Aerobic versus anaerobic fate of pyruvate.

blocks.title: Lactate production from anaerobic glycolysis
blocks.prompt: Ischaemic tissue metabolises 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g per mole) anaerobically. How much lactate and net ATP is formed?

steps.text: Moles of glucose = 18 g / 180 g per mole = 0.10 mol.
One glucose gives 2 pyruvate, which become 2 lactate, so lactate = 2 x 0.10 = 0.20 mol.
Net ATP is 2 per glucose, so net ATP = 2 x 0.10 = 0.20 mol.

blocks.answer: 0.20 mol lactate and 0.20 mol net ATP. Large lactate output explains lactic acidosis in hypoxic tissue.

blocks.markdown: **Why red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis.** Mature erythrocytes extrude their nucleus and **lose their mitochondria**, so they cannot perform the citric acid cycle or oxidative phosphorylation. Their only way to make ATP is glycolysis ending in lactate, even in the presence of oxygen. That ATP maintains membrane ion pumps (Na+/K+-ATPase), the biconcave shape and membrane lipid turnover. A side branch, the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, makes 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), which lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity. If ATP production fails, as in **pyruvate kinase deficiency**, red cells lose pump function, become rigid and are destroyed in the spleen, causing haemolytic anaemia.

blocks.title: Control of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
blocks.text: PDH is switched off by phosphorylation (by PDH kinase, stimulated by ATP, acetyl-CoA and NADH) and switched on by PDH phosphatase (stimulated by insulin and Ca2+); pyruvate inhibits the kinase. PDH deficiency, or thiamine deficiency, causes pyruvate to be diverted to lactate, producing lactic acidosis and neurological injury. Because fat-derived acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies bypass PDH, a high-fat ketogenic diet is used in PDH deficiency, whereas a high-carbohydrate load worsens acidosis.

blocks.title: Remember the three kinases
blocks.text: The irreversible steps are catalysed by hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase. PFK-1 is the committed, rate-limiting step. Do not confuse these with phosphoglycerate kinase, which is reversible.

points: Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate in the cytosol with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH, controlled at hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase.
Aerobically pyruvate is oxidised to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex; anaerobically it is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+.
Red cells have no mitochondria and therefore depend on glycolysis alone for ATP; failure of this supply (for example pyruvate kinase deficiency) causes haemolysis.
PDH is regulated by phosphorylation, and its deficiency causes lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following glycolytic enzymes catalyses an essentially irreversible reaction under physiological conditions?

options.text: Aldolase
Phosphofructokinase-1
Phosphoglycerate kinase
Triose phosphate isomerase

distractorRationale.a: Aldolase works near equilibrium and runs in both directions (it is used in gluconeogenesis).
distractorRationale.b: Correct: PFK-1 is one of the three irreversible, regulated steps.
distractorRationale.c: Phosphoglycerate kinase is reversible and is used by gluconeogenesis.
distractorRationale.d: Triose phosphate isomerase interconverts two triose phosphates at equilibrium.

questions.explanation: Hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase are the three irreversible, regulated enzymes of glycolysis. The remaining reactions are near equilibrium and also operate in gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: What is the essential role of lactate dehydrogenase in a tissue working without oxygen?

options.text: It regenerates NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue
It generates additional ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation
It converts lactate to acetyl-CoA
It transfers pyruvate into mitochondria

questions.correctOptionText: It regenerates NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reducing pyruvate to lactate oxidises NADH back to NAD+, which glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs.
distractorRationale.b: The LDH reaction produces no ATP; ATP comes from phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase.
distractorRationale.c: Acetyl-CoA is made from pyruvate by pyruvate dehydrogenase, not from lactate by LDH.
distractorRationale.d: Pyruvate enters mitochondria via a carrier; LDH is a cytosolic enzyme.

questions.explanation: Without oxygen the respiratory chain cannot reoxidise NADH, so glycolysis would stall for lack of NAD+. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidising NADH to NAD+, allowing the 2 ATP per glucose to continue to be produced.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin raises the concentration of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate in hepatocytes. What is the consequence for glycolysis?

options.text: PFK-1 is activated and glycolytic flux rises
PFK-1 is inhibited and glycolytic flux falls
Pyruvate kinase is directly inhibited
Hexokinase is inhibited through the accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate

questions.correctOptionText: PFK-1 is activated and glycolytic flux rises

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1 and overcomes ATP inhibition.
distractorRationale.b: This is the effect of high ATP or citrate, or of low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate in the fasting state.
distractorRationale.c: Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by phosphorylation, not by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
distractorRationale.d: Glucokinase in the liver is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, and the question concerns PFK-1 regulation.

questions.explanation: In the fed state insulin raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which allosterically activates PFK-1 and stimulates glycolysis. It also inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase in the opposing pathway, so the liver does not run both at once.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old neonate has jaundice and anaemia from haemolysis. Red cell enzyme studies show pyruvate kinase deficiency. Which mechanism best explains the haemolysis?

options.text: Red cells cannot generate enough ATP by glycolysis, so membrane pumps fail and the cells are removed
Red cells cannot make NADPH to protect against oxidants
Red cells accumulate excess ATP that damages the membrane
Red cells cannot make acetyl-CoA from pyruvate

questions.correctOptionText: Red cells cannot generate enough ATP by glycolysis, so membrane pumps fail and the cells are removed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with no mitochondria the red cell depends on glycolysis for ATP, and pyruvate kinase generates one of its ATP-producing steps.
distractorRationale.b: NADPH depends on the pentose phosphate pathway (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase), not on pyruvate kinase.
distractorRationale.c: Pyruvate kinase deficiency lowers ATP; it does not raise it.
distractorRationale.d: Red cells have no mitochondria and never make acetyl-CoA, so this is not the cause of the injury.

questions.explanation: Red cells have no mitochondria and make ATP only by glycolysis, so loss of pyruvate kinase cuts ATP production. Without ATP the Na+/K+-ATPase and other pumps fail, the cells become rigid and are destroyed prematurely, giving haemolytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A boy with pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency has recurrent lactic acidosis, which worsens after high-carbohydrate meals. A paediatric metabolic team proposes a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet. What is the biochemical rationale?

options.text: Fat and ketone bodies supply acetyl-CoA without needing pyruvate dehydrogenase, and less glucose reduces pyruvate diverted to lactate
Fat raises PDH phosphatase activity and restores the enzyme
Fat provides glucose through gluconeogenesis from fatty acids
Fat stimulates lactate dehydrogenase to clear lactate

questions.correctOptionText: Fat and ketone bodies supply acetyl-CoA without needing pyruvate dehydrogenase, and less glucose reduces pyruvate diverted to lactate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-oxidation and ketone body metabolism make acetyl-CoA independently of PDH, and reducing glucose load reduces pyruvate and lactate formation.
distractorRationale.b: Acetyl-CoA from fat actually activates PDH kinase and does not repair a genetic defect.
distractorRationale.c: Even-chain fatty acids cannot give net glucose, so this is not the rationale.
distractorRationale.d: LDH is not induced by fat, and increasing LDH activity would not treat the underlying defect.

questions.explanation: When PDH is deficient, pyruvate from glucose cannot enter the citric acid cycle and is reduced to lactate. Acetyl-CoA generated from fatty acids and ketone bodies bypasses PDH, so fuelling the cycle with fat while limiting carbohydrate lowers the lactate burden.

questions.stem: True or false: mature red blood cells generate most of their ATP by oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Mature red cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot carry out oxidative phosphorylation or the citric acid cycle. Their ATP comes entirely from glycolysis, ending in lactate.

questions.stem: A strenuously exercising muscle metabolises 90 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g per mole) entirely by anaerobic glycolysis to lactate. How many moles of lactate are produced?
questions.explanation: 90 g / 180 g per mole = 0.50 mol glucose. Each glucose yields 2 pyruvate and therefore 2 lactate, so lactate = 2 x 0.50 = 1.0 mol. Large lactate output of this kind is what acidifies muscle and plasma during hypoxia or hard exercise.

questions.stem: A suspension of red cells consumes glucose at 3.0 mmol per hour, all via glycolysis to lactate (ignore the 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shunt). Using the net ATP yield per glucose of anaerobic glycolysis, what is the rate of net ATP production?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP per glucose (4 produced minus 2 invested). At 3.0 mmol glucose per hour the net ATP production is 2 x 3.0 = 6.0 mmol per hour, and this is the sole ATP supply the red cell has to run its pumps.

questions.stem: Name the three irreversible reactions of glycolysis, and explain how PFK-1 is regulated by energy status.
markingGuide: PFK-1 is the committed, rate-limiting step
Inhibited by high ATP and citrate (energy and fuel plentiful)
Activated by AMP (energy low) and by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (the potent activator, raised by insulin)
questions.explanation: The three kinase steps release large amounts of free energy, which makes them irreversible and suitable as regulatory points. PFK-1 is the main control, so glycolytic flux rises when energy is low (AMP) or insulin is high and falls when ATP and citrate show that energy and fuel are plentiful.

questions.stem: Compare the fate of pyruvate under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, and use this to explain why red blood cells always produce lactate even when oxygen is plentiful.
markingGuide: Aerobic: pyruvate enters mitochondria and is oxidised to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, then the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
Anaerobic: lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate in the cytosol
LDH regenerates NAD+ so glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase can continue
Anaerobic yield is 2 ATP per glucose compared with about 30 to 32 aerobically
Red cells have no mitochondria so pyruvate cannot enter the citric acid cycle or PDH
Therefore red cells depend on glycolysis for ATP and release lactate regardless of oxygen supply
questions.explanation: Whether pyruvate is oxidised or reduced depends on whether mitochondria and oxygen are available to reoxidise NADH. Red cells lack mitochondria, so their NADH can only be reoxidised by LDH, making lactate the obligatory end product even in well-oxygenated blood.
